name: Strife as 'father of all' and cosmic justice
plain_explanation: Heraclitus believed conflict ('strife' or 'war') is necessary and even good, since it is strife between opposites that produces the world's harmony; but this strife is not chaotic, because an impersonal justice (the Erinys, or Furies) keeps it within fixed bounds, for example preventing the sun from 'overstepping his measures'.
precise_definition: Heraclitus's doctrine that 'war is the father of all and king of all' and that 'strife is justice' -- conflict between opposites is both the source of all coming-to-be and passing-away and itself subject to an impersonal, quasi-legal cosmic order that prevents any one side from permanently winning.
why_it_mattered: Extends Anaximander's earlier notion of cosmic justice (Chapter II) into a positive doctrine that conflict itself, properly bounded, is the engine of order rather than merely a disturbance of it.
historical_origin: Heraclitus's own fragments, including his praise of Homer's rival Homer being 'wrong' to wish strife would perish from the world.
examples: 'We must know that war is common to all and strife is justice, and that all things come into being and pass away through strife.'
'The sun will not overstep his measures; if he does, the Erinys, the handmaids of Justice, will find him out.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Heraclitus's aristocratic contempt for the Ephesian democracy and his praise of war are directly linked, in the text, to this metaphysical valorization of strife.
